label: Geometric Manifolds
notes: Open by framing the chapter. A geometric structure is local model data plus transition maps in a model group. Holonomy is the global residue of those transitions. The deck follows printed pages 109 through 208 and covers pseudogroups, triangulations, developing maps, discrete actions, bundles and connections, contact structures, and the eight three-dimensional model geometries.

label: (G,X)-Structures
notes: Define a (G,X)-structure. Choose a model space X and a group G acting on it. A (G,X)-manifold is a manifold with an atlas of X-charts whose transitions lie in G. The pseudogroup viewpoint axiomatizes this: charts plus restrictions plus composition produce transition maps with values in G.

label: Triangulations
notes: Triangulations are useful only when local link tests certify that the glued space is actually a manifold. For a three-dimensional triangulation, every vertex link must be a two-sphere; otherwise the gluing has an orbifold point or a non-manifold singularity. The notebook test checks the smallest case: a vertex in a single tetrahedron has triangular link.

label: Developing Maps
notes: A developing map unrolls local charts along paths in the universal cover and records the mismatch after closing a loop as the holonomy. Completeness becomes geometric: the developing map should cover the whole model space, and the holonomy should act properly. The visual unrolls four chart patches and records the developed image.

label: Discrete Actions
notes: Quotient manifolds behave well only when the group action separates nearby translates correctly. The sampler places a square fundamental domain in the plane and translates by a small lattice. The overlap count is a finite proxy for proper discontinuity: only finitely many translates can meet a compact test region.

label: Bundles and Connections
notes: Bundles add a fiber to every base point; connections specify horizontal motion. A standard contact one-form alpha equals dz minus y dx illustrates the contact structure: the plane field defined by the kernel of alpha is maximally nonintegrable. The chapter introduces these as refinements of the basic (G,X) story.

label: Eight Geometries
notes: Present the eight model geometries for three dimensions: E^3, S^3, H^3, S^2 x R, H^2 x R, Nil, Sol, and SL2(R)-tilde. The classification board separates by curvature, product/fibration behavior, and Lie-group structure. It is not a list to memorize; it is a routing table for which structures a closed 3-manifold can support.

label: Smoothability
notes: Comment on PL and smooth structures. In dimensions one through three, PL and smooth categories agree, so triangulations and smooth structures are interchangeable. In higher dimensions this fails. The chapter records this fact so that three-manifold topology can move freely between triangulated and smooth pictures.

label: Holonomy Lab
notes: Walk through the applied lab. Compare three toy holonomy generators on the Euclidean plane: a translation acts freely, a rotation has a fixed point, and a hyperbolic scaling expands and contracts. The lab illustrates why completeness, proper discontinuity, and discreteness are independent filters on the quotient construction.

label: Recap
notes: Close with the chapter takeaways. A geometric structure is local model data plus transition maps; holonomy is the global residue. Triangulations work only when link tests certify manifoldness. Bundles, connections, contact structures, and PL/smooth structures refine the basic story. The eight model geometries are the classification board for three-dimensional homogeneity.
